newsitem.title: CHINA: Hong Kong little changed one month into China rule.
newsitem.headline: Hong Kong little changed one month into China rule.

text.p: Apart from the rare flutter of a Chinese red flag on a public building, nothing much else would tell you Hong Kong is part of China, one month into Beijing rule.

The more authoritarian tone of government, polemics over an ousted elected legislature, screams over a dilution of civil rights and potential constitutional crises have had little impact on Hong Kong's 6.4 million, mostly Chinese people.
Opinion polls show buoyant public confidence in the future.
The hustle and bustle of this Asian economic wonder, the seventh largest trading economy with the highest per capita ownership of Rolls Royce cars in the world, goes on.

Government House, the seat of 156 years of British colonial rule, a neo-classical mansion set on the verdant slopes of Hong Kong Island where the Union Jack flew proudly until a month ago, has a sad, abandoned air. Leaves clutter its empty driveway.
It is soon to become a museum and state guest house. The Governor's Rolls Royce is to be auctioned off.

Perhaps the biggest change is the absence of its feisty and colourful colonial Governor Chris Patten, whose five years at the helm awoke Hong Kong from its political apathy, brought in more democracy, and unleashed fierce debate that polarised the territory into rival pro-China and pro-democracy camps.
"I think Chris Patten did a lot for Hong Kong but the place will become a lot less divided now that he has gone," said a government official.

"It's so quiet in Hong Kong now that people are starting to miss Patten because he made the place so lively," jested Feng Xiliang, a veteran Chinese newspaper editor and consultant to the territory's flagship South China Morning Post.

Hong Kong's famed Wanchai red light district may have lost the pocket money of British garrison soldiers, now long gone, but scores of U.S. warships will still bring tens of thousands of American sailors and soldiers on recreational port calls.
The stock exchange has shrugged off any worries that business might have had about Chinese rule. Its key index rocketed beyond the magic 16,000-point barrier this week.
There has never been much correlation between political events and sharp short-term movements in the Hang Seng index.
"Not that much has changed. Political risk hasn't changed," said Richard Margolis, head of research at Merrill Lynch Asia.
"All the gloom and doom scenarios have not come to pass," Margolis told Reuters. "But it would be premature to declare victory after only 30 days," he cautioned.
There have been no arrests of pro-democracy politicians, although they have been ousted from the legislature and replaced by China-appointed, unelected lawmakers.

There have been no midnight calls by men in leather coats at the doors of Chinese dissidents in exile. And no Tiananmen-style crackdowns by China's newly installed, 4,700-strong People's Liberation Army (PLA) garrison.

"When you look around, you feel that nothing much has changed. And that's probably the best kind of change one could have hoped for," said Hugh Davies, Britain's senior envoy in charge of handover negotiations with China.
Not that there are no problems lurking in the hallways.
The government of China-appointed leader Tung Chee-hwa escaped a constitutional crisis this week when a court crushed a challenge to the legal and constitutional system now in place.

Further challenges of this ilk lie ahead, some linked to Tung's moves to freeze trade union rights, others linked to his plans to deport child illegal immigrants, and yet others associated with his plans to substantially reduce direct democracy in legislative elections slated for next May.
Britain called on Tung's government on Wednesday to hold "free and fair" elections as soon as possible.
One problem feared by pro-democracy politicians -- overt interference from Beijing -- has not materialised so far.
In a reassuring signal the Chinese Foreign Ministry's new Commissioner in Hong Kong, Ma Yuzhen, said this week that Beijing would grant Hong Kong more foreign policy powers.
There were also signs that China's traditional Communist Party watchdog in the territory, the Xinhua News Agency Branch, was to undergo a revamp, reducing its role.

The PLA has kept its head down. After a series of minor public relations gaffes committed out of pure naivet, the garrison is now planning to open a public relations office and has covered its armoured cars with tarpaulins.
Britain's colonial officials have gone and its diplomats are settling into a more conventional role in a newly opened Consulate-General, London's largest in the world.
"We are glad the handover is over. Other consulates are treating us like real diplomats now, we are integrating into the Hong Kong diplomatic community," said one member of the consulate's staff.
Derek Fatchet, the British minister responsible for Hong Kong policy, said in London on Wednesday it was time to look to the future and forge a new relationship with China.
"We're not going to hark into the past, we're going to move forward...in a positive and constructive way building up the new partnerships and new relationships," he told Hong Kong radio.
